# FIG. 1

Exploded perspective view of a reusable passive cold-chain carrier, black line work on white, patent drawing style. The four bodies are separated vertically along a common upright axis, seen from slightly above one front corner so the top of each lower body is visible. Keep all line work well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

- Insulated outer shell 10: an open-topped rectangular box with visible wall thickness, its interior open and empty in this view. Its rim, the upper edge 16, is a narrow flat band running around the whole top of the box.
- Removable product tray 20: an open-topped rectangular pan, smaller in plan than the shell 10 and with lower walls, floating directly above the shell 10.
- Perforation 26: small through holes in the tray 20, shown schematically.
- Removable thermal module 40: a flat rectangular assembly floating above the tray 20 and about the same outline in plan, shown schematically as a shallow rectangular frame body of visible thickness that is open at the centre of its width, and two upright slab-like bodies held within the frame body on opposite sides of that central open region.
- Insulated lid 60: a rectangular slab floating above the module 40, matching the shell 10 in plan, tipped in the same perspective so that its underside is visible. A compressible lid gasket 64 is drawn on that underside as a continuous band set in from the perimeter and running all the way around it.
- Depending indexing rib 62: a short straight rib projecting downward from the underside of the lid 60, shown schematically, inboard of the gasket 64 and above the module 40.

- The tray 20, the module 40, and the lid 60 are each smaller than or equal in plan to the opening of the shell 10 and are aligned one above the other, so that they would descend into or onto the shell 10.
- The upper edge 16 faces the compressible lid gasket 64.

A broken cutting-plane line crosses each of the lid 60, the module 40, the tray 20, and the shell 10 horizontally at the same position across the common upright axis, each segment running from a point clear of the left outer wall of that body to a point clear of its right outer wall, parallel to the front portion of the upper edge 16. Together the segments are line 2-2, the same section designation being repeated at each end of the line, and an arrow at each end points toward the rear, the direction in which the section of FIG. 2 is viewed. The section designation of line 2-2 is drawing annotation and is not a reference numeral of this sheet.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10

- 60
- 62
- 64

All eight findings are fixed, and the numeral table, drawing descriptions, description, claims and figure briefs remain in step.

- **FIG-2 (critical):** the condensate trough is no longer described as formed in the upper surface of the floor slab; the bullet now matches FIG-5's neutral wording, so both briefs describe the same part the same way.
- **Description ¶25 (major):** the assertion about what the peripheral outlet openings 50 face when the module is out of position is gone; the supported point that the descending limb is blocked and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box remains.
- **FIG-3:** the indexing rib 62 is now a downwardly projecting hatched tongue on the underside of the lid 60, shown schematically, with no one-piece construction and no clearance-fit statement.
- **FIG-1:** the gasket 64 is a continuous band shown schematically and positioned to face the upper edge 16, with no inward offset; the shell 10, tray 20 and lid 60 outlines now carry the schematic qualifier used elsewhere in the brief. The rib bullet's position relative to the gasket went with the offset, since it depended on it; the rib is still located above the module 40.
- **FIG-6:** spring 86 is a spring shown schematically as connected loops acting outward on the stem 82, without a spring type or a loaded-state instruction.
- **Description ¶9:** the loading result and the separate-ducting comparison are gone; the paragraph now states only that the side supply passages 30 and the lower return passage 28 are formed by the position the tray takes up in the shell.
- **Background ¶1:** "carriers" meaning transport companies is now "couriers", so "carrier" means the claimed device throughout.

No claim was altered. Every brief remains under 2800 characters (longest is FIG-1 at 2710) and no sheet lists more than eight numerals.

input.summary: Fixed all eight findings without touching the claim backbone: removed the FIG-2 statement that the condensate trough is formed in the shell-floor slab, deleted the undisclosed misregistered geometry from description paragraph 25, removed the untraced loading result and separate-ducting comparison from paragraph 9, changed Background "carriers" to "couriers" so the defined device term is unambiguous, and reduced four figure-brief over-specifications (rib construction and clearance fit in FIG-3, gasket radial position and unqualified body outlines in FIG-1, spring type and compression state in FIG-6) to labelled depiction conventions.
reasoning: The critical item was a flow-boundary assertion, not a drawing style question: saying the trough is formed in the upper surface of the floor slab beside the tray puts a condensate feature inside the lower end of the disclosed air path. FIG-5 already carried the neutral wording the source supports, so matching FIG-2 to it removes the assertion and the inconsistency in one move. The channel remains depicted, so claim 6 and the condensate paragraph keep their figure support.

Description paragraph 25 previously said where the peripheral outlet openings 50 discharge when the module is misplaced. The disclosure describes only the registered condition, so the misregistered geometry had no source. Deleting the clause leaves the supported failure statement intact, which is what the registration argument in the specification actually rests on: the path exists only when the openings overlap the passages, and a misplaced module gives no outward sign. That rationale is still in place ahead of any later need for it.

Paragraph 9 asserted a servicing result and a negative comparison to separate ducting. Neither is in the inventor's words, and neither supports a claim limitation, so removing them costs no scope while keeping the structural point that the passages are defined by the position the tray takes up in the shell, which is the antecedent for the passages recited in claim 1.

The Background used carrier for the transport company while the claims use carrier for the apparatus. Changing that one instance to courier makes the defined term single-valued across title, field, summary, description, claims and abstract without altering the prior-art discussion.

For the four minor figure findings I kept every disclosed body and relationship and removed only the invented specificity: one-piece rib construction and a clearance fit for a functional joint, the gasket's inward offset from the lid edge, the spring's type and loaded state, and the implicit shape assertions in the three main FIG-1 outlines. Each item is now a labelled schematic convention, so nothing in the application text or the numeral table had to move to accommodate it. Removing the gasket offset also required dropping 'inboard of the gasket 64' from the FIG-1 rib bullet, since that position was defined only by the offset just deleted; the rib is still placed above the module.
No numeral changed hands this round, so the eight-per-sheet distribution set last round still holds, and every brief stayed inside the 2800-character limit after the edits.

draft/08-detailed-description.md paragraph 25: deleted 'the peripheral outlet openings 50 discharge against the tray side walls 24 or against the shell side walls 14,'.

draft/08-detailed-description.md paragraph 9: replaced the loading and separate-ducting sentence with 'The side supply passages 30 and the lower return passage 28 are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10.'
draft/05-background.md paragraph 1: 'handed to one or more carriers' changed to 'handed to one or more couriers'.

figures/FIG-3.md: rib 62 is now 'a downwardly projecting hatched tongue on the underside of the lid 60, shown schematically', with the clearance-fit clause removed and the facing side surfaces retained.

figures/FIG-1.md: gasket 64 now 'shown schematically as a continuous band running all the way around it and positioned to face the upper edge 16'; 'shown schematically' added to the shell 10, tray 20 and lid 60 bullets; 'inboard of the gasket 64' removed from the rib 62 bullet.

figures/FIG-6.md: spring 86 now 'a spring shown schematically as a series of connected loops ... acting on the stem 82 in the outward direction', with the spring type and the compression-state instruction removed.
input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, characterize or design around, and the Background carries no citations. The point of distinction the specification develops is unchanged by this revision: the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel as the lid closes shifts the removable thermal module into the position where the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the closed, fan-free circulation path around the removable tray and between two opposed phase-change cassettes is established by the act of closing rather than by the packer's aim. The paragraph explaining the problem this solves, a displaced module that silently reduces the carrier to a plain insulated box, is retained in the description. Because no search was run, the art available to this draft may be incomplete.
input.answer: Every mechanical check item and reviewer finding is resolved. FIG-2 no longer states that the condensate trough is formed in the upper surface of the shell-floor slab, so it now matches FIG-5's neutral depiction of shallow condensate channel 70. The Background now says couriers where it meant transport companies, so carrier means only the claimed device across the application. In the drawings, the indexing rib is no longer integral with the lid and no longer has a specified clearance fit in the mating channel; the lid gasket has no stated inward offset and is identified as facing the upper edge 16; the shell, tray and lid outlines carry the schematic qualifier; and spring 86 is shown schematically as connected loops acting outward on the stem, with no spring type or compression state. No claim, numeral definition or disclosed embodiment was altered, the reference-numeral table is unchanged and still fully used, each brief's numeral list still matches what it verbalizes, no sheet lists more than eight numerals, and every brief is under 2800 characters.

structured_output.summary: Fixed all eight findings without touching the claim backbone: removed the FIG-2 statement that the condensate trough is formed in the shell-floor slab, deleted the undisclosed misregistered geometry from description paragraph 25, removed the untraced loading result and separate-ducting comparison from paragraph 9, changed Background "carriers" to "couriers" so the defined device term is unambiguous, and reduced four figure-brief over-specifications (rib construction and clearance fit in FIG-3, gasket radial position and unqualified body outlines in FIG-1, spring type and compression state in FIG-6) to labelled depiction conventions.
reasoning: The critical item was a flow-boundary assertion, not a drawing style question: saying the trough is formed in the upper surface of the floor slab beside the tray puts a condensate feature inside the lower end of the disclosed air path. FIG-5 already carried the neutral wording the source supports, so matching FIG-2 to it removes the assertion and the inconsistency in one move. The channel remains depicted, so claim 6 and the condensate paragraph keep their figure support.

Description paragraph 25 previously said where the peripheral outlet openings 50 discharge when the module is misplaced. The disclosure describes only the registered condition, so the misregistered geometry had no source. Deleting the clause leaves the supported failure statement intact, which is what the registration argument in the specification actually rests on: the path exists only when the openings overlap the passages, and a misplaced module gives no outward sign. That rationale is still in place ahead of any later need for it.

Paragraph 9 asserted a servicing result and a negative comparison to separate ducting. Neither is in the inventor's words, and neither supports a claim limitation, so removing them costs no scope while keeping the structural point that the passages are defined by the position the tray takes up in the shell, which is the antecedent for the passages recited in claim 1.

The Background used carrier for the transport company while the claims use carrier for the apparatus. Changing that one instance to courier makes the defined term single-valued across title, field, summary, description, claims and abstract without altering the prior-art discussion.

For the four minor figure findings I kept every disclosed body and relationship and removed only the invented specificity: one-piece rib construction and a clearance fit for a functional joint, the gasket's inward offset from the lid edge, the spring's type and loaded state, and the implicit shape assertions in the three main FIG-1 outlines. Each item is now a labelled schematic convention, so nothing in the application text or the numeral table had to move to accommodate it. Removing the gasket offset also required dropping 'inboard of the gasket 64' from the FIG-1 rib bullet, since that position was defined only by the offset just deleted; the rib is still placed above the module.

## Reviewer findings

- **[critical] Figure briefs verbalize an undisclosed runout direction for the peripheral outlet opening 50** (figures/FIG-4.md bullet "Peripheral outlet opening 50" and closing relationship line; figures/FIG-2.md bullet "Removable) - The peripheral outlet opening is a functional port on a flow boundary. Both briefs state which face of the frame the port runs out through and in which direction it discharges. The disclosure discloses the port's existence and its registration with the side supply passages, but says nothing about the face it pierces or the direction it opens; a downwardly opening peripheral port over the top of the passage is equally consistent with the source. Under this preflight, runout direction of a port is substantive even where the brief calls the geometry schematic, so the direction must be removed and replaced with a minimally specific communication statement.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-4.md replace the bullet with: "Peripheral outlet opening 50: a gap in the periphery of the frame 42 at the lower end of the duct 48, through which the duct 48 communicates with the upper end of the side supply passage 30, shown schematically." and replace the relationship line with: "The duct 48 communicates with the upper end of the side supply passage 30 through the peripheral outlet opening 50, the opening 50 overlapping the upper end of that passage so that the two are in open communication." In figures/FIG-2.md replace the clause with: "each communicating at its lower end with one side supply passage 30 through a peripheral outlet opening 50, a gap in the periphery of the module 40 overlapping the upper end of that passage."
- **[major] FIG-1 gives the thermal module the tray's plan outline, contradicting FIG-2 and FIG-4** (figures/FIG-1.md bullet "Removable thermal module 40") - FIG-1 states the module has about the same plan outline as the tray. The side supply passages lie outboard of the tray side walls, and the resilient feet bear on ledges on the inward-facing surface of the shell side walls. A module confined to the tray's plan outline can neither overlap the side supply passages with its peripheral outlet openings (FIG-2, FIG-4) nor reach the shell ledges with its resilient feet (FIG-4). The three briefs cannot all be rendered as written.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-1.md replace "floating above the tray 20 and about the same outline in plan" with "floating above the tray 20 and about the same outline in plan as the opening of the shell 10, so that it spans the tray 20 and the space at each side of the tray 20".
- **[major] FIG-2 flow-arrow route is geometrically impossible against the brief's own definitions of 26 and 28** (figures/FIG-2.md bullet "Flow arrows") - The brief defines perforation 26 as gaps through the tray and lower return passage 28 as the space between the tray bottom panel and the floor slab. The arrow bullet then instructs that air passes through the perforations 26 and only afterwards travels along the lower return passage 28 and into the tray 20. Air that has passed through the perforations is already inside the tray and cannot then travel along the passage beneath the tray and re-enter it. The recited order in 06-summary, 08-detailed-description, claim 1 and claim 12 is verbatim source language and should stand; the drawing brief must simply stop asserting an impossible strict sequence.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-2.md replace the tail of the flow-arrow bullet with: "... through the peripheral outlet openings 50 into the side supply passages 30, down each passage 30, and through the perforations 26 and the lower return passage 28 back into the interior of the tray 20, the arrows forming a closed circuit."
- **[major] FIG-3 closes the frame underside on each side of the inlet while the ducts and opening 56 require it open** (figures/FIG-3.md bullet "Central inlet opening 46", read against FIG-3.md bullet "Downward guide duct 48" and figures/FI) - Read literally, "closing the underside of the frame 42 on each side of it" closes the whole underside outboard of the central inlet. That contradicts the same brief's requirement that each duct be open at its lower end, and contradicts FIG-4, which places a downwardly opening condensate discharge opening 56 in that underside at the lower end of the duct. The renderer is given mutually exclusive instructions about the same flow boundary.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-3.md replace the trailing clause with: "a lower web portion of the frame 42 closing the underside of the frame 42 beneath each cassette 44 on each side of the opening 46, the underside of the frame 42 remaining open at the lower end of each duct 48."
- **[major] FIG-3 asserts communication between the inter-cassette space and the ducts without specifying any route** (figures/FIG-3.md relationship line following the bullet list) - The brief states that the space between the cassettes communicates with both ducts, but the bullets give no gap or opening through which it does so: the cassettes are "held within the frame 42" between the lower web portions and the upper horizontal web, and each duct is bounded by the cassette's outboard surface and the frame's outboard web. As written the two spaces are separated by solid cassette bodies, so the asserted communication is not renderable. The disclosed flow compels a crossover, and because the ducts are descending the crossover must be at their upper ends, so a minimally specific gap can be stated without adding undisclosed substance.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-3.md append to the "Phase-change cassette 44" bullet: "Each cassette 44 stops short of the upper web of the frame 42, leaving a blank open gap between its upper end and the underside of that web through which the space between the cassettes 44 communicates with the upper end of the duct 48 on that side."
- **[major] Untraced limitation: the removable product tray lifts out "with a payload in it"** (draft/09-claims.md claim 5 and claim 15; draft/08-detailed-description.md, "Overview of the carrier", third paragraph) - No inventor passage states that the tray is lifted out of the shell with the payload inside it. The disclosure states that products are placed in the tray and that the tray is removable and is removed, but the removal-with-payload result is the drafter's addition. An inherency argument is available, which is why this is graded major rather than critical, but as an express claim limitation and description statement it has no affirmative source passage. The companion recitation that the module "lifts out ... as one piece with both phase-change cassettes" is traced to "a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes" plus "a removable thermal module" and needs no change.
  - Suggested fix: Claim 5: delete "with a payload in it", ending "... and the removable product tray thereafter lifts out of the insulated outer shell." Claim 15: delete "with the payload in it", ending "... and thereafter lifting the removable product tray out of the insulated outer shell." Description: replace the sentence with "The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out." Also delete "with the payload in it" from the sentence in "Method of passively conditioning a payload" reading "and the removable product tray 20 is lifted out with the payload in it."
- **[minor] Untraced servicing step: reconditioning the phase-change cassettes between journeys** (draft/08-detailed-description.md, "Method of passively conditioning a payload", last paragraph) - The disclosure states only that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame for use; it never states that the cassettes are reconditioned between journeys. The step is plausibly inherent in a reusable carrier, but no affirmative passage recites it. It is not claimed, so deleting it costs nothing.
  - Suggested fix: Delete ", the phase-change cassettes 44 are reconditioned," so the sentence reads "Between journeys the removable absorbent wick 72 is withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position."
- **[minor] FIG-6 asserts a thermal coupling across structure it expressly omits** (figures/FIG-6.md view note, bullet "Phase-change cassette 44", and first relationship line) - The brief tells the renderer to omit the structure between the shell side wall and the cassette, then instructs that the inner end of the stem 82 is thermally coupled to the cassette 44. With the intervening region blank, no coupling can be depicted; the instruction is unrenderable as written. The disclosed fact (thermal coupling) should be carried by a lead-line relationship rather than by an unshowable contact.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-6.md replace the tail of the cassette bullet with "..., the inner end of the stem 82 reaching toward it, the structure between them being omitted for clarity", and replace the first relationship line with "The stem 82 extends from the interior of the indicator 80 through the thickness of the shell side wall 14, its inner end reaching the cassette 44 to which it is thermally coupled, the intervening structure being omitted."
- **[minor] Closed-condition section of FIG. 2 is taken on a line drawn across the exploded FIG. 1** (draft/07-drawings.md, FIG. 2 sentence; figures/FIG-1.md cutting-plane paragraph; figures/FIG-2.md heading line) - FIG. 1 is an exploded view in which the four bodies are separated along the upright axis, yet the cutting-plane line drawn across those separated bodies is cited as producing FIG. 2, which shows the carrier closed with the gasket compressed between the lid and the shell walls. The change of state between the source view and the resulting view is not acknowledged, which reads as an inconsistency between the two views. The designation itself is consistent (line 2-2 repeated at both ends with arrows), so only the state needs to be stated.
  - Suggested fix: In draft/07-drawings.md write: "FIG. 2 is a schematic vertical sectional view of the carrier in a closed condition, taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 1 with the parts of FIG. 1 assembled, showing ...". In figures/FIG-2.md write: "Schematic vertical section through the closed carrier, taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 1 with the parts of FIG. 1 assembled". In figures/FIG-1.md append to the cutting-plane paragraph: "the segments together indicating the plane of the section of FIG. 2, which shows the bodies assembled and the carrier closed."

Fix every listed item before returning. If an advisory is a false positive, make

In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright attitude of use, in which the insulated lid is uppermost. The described embodiments illustrate the invention and do not limit it. FIG. 1 through FIG. 6 show one carrier, each view showing the parts that view is concerned with, and a part introduced in one view is referred to elsewhere in this description whether or not it is shown in every view.

## Overview of the carrier

Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 2, and FIG. 5, a reusable passive cold-chain carrier includes an insulated outer shell 10, a removable product tray 20, a removable thermal module 40, and an insulated lid 60. The insulated outer shell 10 has a shell floor 12, shell side walls 14 rising from the shell floor 12, and an upper edge 16 at the top of the shell side walls 14. The insulated outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are of insulating construction, and the carrier can be returned for reuse.

Referring also to FIG. 5, the removable product tray 20 receives the payload. The removable product tray 20 has tray side walls 24 and tray feet 22. The tray feet 22 stand on the shell floor 12 and suspend the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12, so that a lower return passage 28 remains under the removable product tray 20. The tray side walls 24 are spaced inward from the shell side walls 14 to form two side supply passages 30. The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through the removable product tray 20.

The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit, with the payload in it, once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out. The side supply passages 30 and the lower return passage 28 are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10.

## The removable thermal module

Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the removable thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 holding two opposed phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 is a rigid frame body. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.

The rigid spacer frame 42 includes a central inlet opening 46 at the centre of the rigid spacer frame 42 and facing the product region within the removable product tray 20, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the phase-change cassettes 44, and peripheral outlet openings 50. Each phase-change cassette 44 is a cassette of phase-change material that is conditioned before use, and the two phase-change cassettes 44 are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening 46 with their faces mutually opposed. Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.

Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once.

## The registered passive circulation path

The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.

In use, warm air rising from a product region within the removable product tray 20 enters the central inlet opening 46, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, descends through the downward guide ducts 48, enters the side supply passages 30, passes through the perforations 26 in the removable product tray 20, and returns through the lower return passage 28 to the product region. The path is closed on itself and surrounds the removable product tray 20 on the sides and underneath, so that cooled air reaches the payload around and beneath the removable product tray 20.

The path exists only when the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position, the descending limb of the path is blocked, and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box. This is the failure that the registration described below is directed to, and it is a failure that gives no outward sign, because a removable thermal module 40 that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.

## Lid-driven registration and retention

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 3, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.

A compressible lid gasket 64 on the insulated lid 60 seals against the upper edge 16 of the insulated outer shell 10 after registration. The order of these two events matters. The depending indexing rib 62 engages the mating channel 52 and completes the registration before the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge 16, so that the removable thermal module 40 is free to be shifted by the depending indexing rib 62 and is not being asked to move after the interior has been closed off. Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior.

Referring to FIG. 4, the same closing movement presses resilient feet 54 of the rigid spacer frame 42 against ledges 18 of the insulated outer shell 10, so that the removable thermal module 40 cannot lift away from the removable product tray 20 during transport. That pressing holds the removable thermal module 40 down against handling, tilting, and vibration in transit, which would otherwise let the removable thermal module 40 rise and break the overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 50 and the side supply passages 30.

Registration and retention are thus produced by the same movement that a user has to make in any event. Nothing has to be latched, clamped, or checked separately, and there is no state in which the carrier is closed and sealed but the circulation path is not established.

## Condensate handling and the removable wick

Referring to FIG. 4 and FIG. 5, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.

The removable absorbent wick 72 has a pull tab 74. The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44. Routine servicing between journeys therefore does not require handling of the phase-change cassettes 44, which are conditioned items and are not to be opened. Withdrawing the removable absorbent wick 72 from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and placing a replacement absorbent wick in the shallow condensate channel 70 restores the carrier for the next journey.

## Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 6, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction, and the temperature-responsive latch 84 retains the indicator stem 82 against that action while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.

If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette 44 cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The value of this behaviour is that a payload which was warmed part way through a journey and then cooled again arrives at a temperature that looks correct, and the contents alone give the recipient no way to know what happened. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 records the event in the structure of the carrier and holds the record until a person opens the carrier and deliberately resets it.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The circulation path is the same whether the indicator stem 82 is retained or has moved to the latched exposed position. The thermal condition being reported is taken directly from a phase-change cassette 44, that is, from the reserve that actually conditions the payload, and no electrical power, battery, or logging device is required for the indication.

## Method of passively conditioning a payload

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes 44 are fitted to the rigid spacer frame 42 to form the removable thermal module 40, products are placed in the removable product tray 20, the removable product tray 20 is placed in the insulated outer shell 10 on its tray feet 22, the removable thermal module 40 is placed above the removable product tray 20, and the insulated lid 60 is closed. Closing the insulated lid 60 brings the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 52, shifts the removable thermal module 40 into the registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30, presses the resilient feet 54 against the ledges 18, and compresses the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 after that registration. Air then circulates passively along the path described above for the duration of the journey.

At the destination the insulated lid 60 is opened, the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out, and the removable product tray 20 is lifted out with the payload in it. Between journeys the removable absorbent wick 72 is withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, the phase-change cassettes 44 are reconditioned, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position.

## Variations

The removable absorbent wick 72 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features. A carrier may be built with the registered passive circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with either optional feature separately, or with both. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another where the combination is physically consistent. The claims that follow define the invention, and each claim is to be read in the light of the whole of this description.

content.text:
All nine findings are fixed and the files remain synchronized.

- **Peripheral outlet opening 50 (critical):** FIG-4 and FIG-2 no longer state which face the port pierces or which way it discharges. Both now say only that the duct communicates with the upper end of the side supply passage through the opening, which overlaps that passage.
- **FIG-1 module plan:** the module now spans the tray and the space at each side of it, matching the overlap in FIG-2 and the resilient foot bearing on the shell ledge in FIG-4.
- **FIG-2 arrows:** the tail no longer asserts an impossible strict order; the arrows pass through the perforations and the lower return passage back into the interior of the tray as a closed circuit. The claim and description recitations, which are source wording, are untouched.
- **FIG-3 frame underside:** a lower web portion closes the underside beneath each cassette, and the underside stays open at the lower end of each duct, which is where FIG-4 puts condensate discharge opening 56.
- **FIG-3 crossover:** each cassette stops short of the upper web, leaving the gap through which the inter-cassette space reaches the upper end of the duct on that side, so the stated communication is now depictable.
- **"with a payload in it":** deleted from claim 5, claim 15 and both description sentences; both claims stand on the removability and stacking order alone.
- **Reconditioning step:** removed from the servicing sentence.
- **FIG-6:** the stem now reaches the cassette it is thermally coupled to, with the intervening structure noted as omitted, so the relationship is carried by the lead line rather than by an unshowable contact.
- **Section state:** FIG. 2 is now taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 1 with the parts of FIG. 1 assembled, in 07-drawings, the FIG-2 heading, and the FIG-1 cutting-plane paragraph.

Every brief is under 2800 characters (longest FIG-2 at 2782), no sheet lists more than eight numerals, and the numeral table is unchanged and fully used.

input.summary: Fixed all nine findings: removed the undisclosed runout direction of peripheral outlet opening 50 from FIG-2 and FIG-4, resolved five figure-brief internal-logic defects (module plan outline in FIG-1, the impossible arrow sequence in FIG-2, the closed frame underside and the unrouted crossover in FIG-3, the unshowable coupling in FIG-6), deleted the untraced "with a payload in it" from claims 5 and 15 and both description sentences, deleted the untraced reconditioning step, and stated the assembled state of the FIG. 2 section in all three places where the section is designated.
reasoning: The critical item was a port geometry statement, not a style question. FIG-2 and FIG-4 both said the opening pierces the outboard face and discharges sideways; the source says only that the openings are peripheral and overlap the side supply passages. Both briefs now state the communication and the overlap without a face or a direction, which keeps every relationship claim 1 and claim 12 rely on while removing the invented runout.

The untraced 'with a payload in it' came out of claim 5, claim 15 and the description. Both claims keep their real content, that the module lifts out as one piece with both cassettes and the tray lifts out afterwards, which is what the disclosed removability and stacking order support. Deleting the payload words costs no scope worth having, since a tray removal step does not become narrower by reciting what is sitting in the tray, and it removes the only claim limitation the review could not trace.

Two FIG-3 defects were mutually reinforcing: the underside was closed everywhere outboard of the inlet, yet each duct had to be open at its lower end and FIG-4 puts condensate discharge opening 56 in that underside. The underside now closes only beneath each cassette and stays open at the lower end of each duct, so one flow boundary is described one way across both sheets.

The crossover gap at the cassette upper ends was added because the brief asserted communication between the inter-cassette space and the ducts with no route by which it could be drawn. The disclosed flow enters the central inlet, divides along the cassette faces and descends the ducts, so with descending ducts the crossover has to be at the upper ends; the gap is the minimally specific way to make the disclosed path renderable. This is drawing depiction only. No corresponding language was added to the description or the claims.

FIG-1's module was confined to the tray's plan outline, which contradicted both the outlet-to-passage overlap and the resilient feet reaching ledges on the shell wall. Widening the module to about the shell opening is forced by the disclosed structure rather than chosen for appearance, so it removes the contradiction without adding a proportion the inventor never gave.

FIG-2's arrow bullet was the only place asserting a strict order that its own definitions made impossible. The claims, summary and description keep the source sequence verbatim, and only the drawing instruction was relaxed to a closed circuit through the perforations and the return passage, so the arrows can be drawn without changing the recited path.

FIG-6 told the renderer to omit the structure between the wall and the cassette and then to show a thermal coupling across it. The stem now reaches the cassette it is thermally coupled to, with the omission stated, so the disclosed coupling is carried by the lead line rather than by contact the view cannot show.

The reconditioning step and the section-state mismatch were both cheap to fix and unclaimed: the servicing sentence now recites only the wick replacement and the indicator reset, and the FIG. 2 section is stated as taken with the parts of FIG. 1 assembled in 07-drawings, the FIG-2 heading and the FIG-1 cutting-plane paragraph, so the exploded source view and the closed resulting view agree.

structured_output.summary: Fixed all nine findings: removed the undisclosed runout direction of peripheral outlet opening 50 from FIG-2 and FIG-4, resolved five figure-brief internal-logic defects (module plan outline in FIG-1, the impossible arrow sequence in FIG-2, the closed frame underside and the unrouted crossover in FIG-3, the unshowable coupling in FIG-6), deleted the untraced "with a payload in it" from claims 5 and 15 and both description sentences, deleted the untraced reconditioning step, and stated the assembled state of the FIG. 2 section in all three places where the section is designated.
reasoning: The critical item was a port geometry statement, not a style question. FIG-2 and FIG-4 both said the opening pierces the outboard face and discharges sideways; the source says only that the openings are peripheral and overlap the side supply passages. Both briefs now state the communication and the overlap without a face or a direction, which keeps every relationship claim 1 and claim 12 rely on while removing the invented runout.

The untraced 'with a payload in it' came out of claim 5, claim 15 and the description. Both claims keep their real content, that the module lifts out as one piece with both cassettes and the tray lifts out afterwards, which is what the disclosed removability and stacking order support. Deleting the payload words costs no scope worth having, since a tray removal step does not become narrower by reciting what is sitting in the tray, and it removes the only claim limitation the review could not trace.

Two FIG-3 defects were mutually reinforcing: the underside was closed everywhere outboard of the inlet, yet each duct had to be open at its lower end and FIG-4 puts condensate discharge opening 56 in that underside. The underside now closes only beneath each cassette and stays open at the lower end of each duct, so one flow boundary is described one way across both sheets.

The crossover gap at the cassette upper ends was added because the brief asserted communication between the inter-cassette space and the ducts with no route by which it could be drawn. The disclosed flow enters the central inlet, divides along the cassette faces and descends the ducts, so with descending ducts the crossover has to be at the upper ends; the gap is the minimally specific way to make the disclosed path renderable. This is drawing depiction only. No corresponding language was added to the description or the claims.

FIG-1's module was confined to the tray's plan outline, which contradicted both the outlet-to-passage overlap and the resilient feet reaching ledges on the shell wall. Widening the module to about the shell opening is forced by the disclosed structure rather than chosen for appearance, so it removes the contradiction without adding a proportion the inventor never gave.

FIG-2's arrow bullet was the only place asserting a strict order that its own definitions made impossible. The claims, summary and description keep the source sequence verbatim, and only the drawing instruction was relaxed to a closed circuit through the perforations and the return passage, so the arrows can be drawn without changing the recited path.

FIG-6 told the renderer to omit the structure between the wall and the cassette and then to show a thermal coupling across it. The stem now reaches the cassette it is thermally coupled to, with the omission stated, so the disclosed coupling is carried by the lead line rather than by contact the view cannot show.

The reconditioning step and the section-state mismatch were both cheap to fix and unclaimed: the servicing sentence now recites only the wick replacement and the indicator reset, and the FIG. 2 section is stated as taken with the parts of FIG. 1 assembled in 07-drawings, the FIG-2 heading and the FIG-1 cutting-plane paragraph, so the exploded source view and the closed resulting view agree.

1	# Previous review - verdict: fail
2	
3	Ledger scope: I traced every claim limitation (claims 1–17), every numeral in draft/numerals.md (10–86), and every structure, relationship, result, position, connection and operating condition in draft/04-field.md through draft/10-abstract.md and figures/FIG-1.md through FIG-6.md to the USER disclosure (input/disclosure.md, mirrored in the single USER passage of input/conversation.md). input/brief.md was used only for formalities (title is a "working title" so the descriptive title is acceptable; "No priority claim" and "No federally sponsored research" match the "Not applicable." cross-reference and government-support sections). prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the Background makes no citation, so nothing needed prior-art tracing.
4	
5	Supported and clean: the four bodies (shell 10 / tray 20 / module 40 / lid 60), tray feet 22 and lower return passage 28, tray side walls 24 spaced inward to form two side supply passages 30, perforations 26, rigid spacer frame 42 with two opposed cassettes 44, central inlet opening 46, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings 50 aligned with the side passages, the full passive flow sequence and "no fan, pump, or powered air mover", depending indexing rib 62 / mating channel 52 registration, gasket 64 sealing against upper edge 16 "after registration", resilient feet 54 on ledges 18, shallow condensate channel 70 with discharge openings 56 at duct lower ends, wick 72 and pull tab 74, and indicator 80/82/84/86 including irreversibility, manual reset and non-control of airflow. Method claims 12–17 map to the disclosed use and servicing sequence. Claims 4 and 5 (cassettes on opposite sides of the inlet; module lifting out as one piece with the tray thereafter) are entailed by "two opposed phase-change cassettes", "divides along faces of the cassettes", "central inlet", and "the spacer frame rests above the product tray", so I did not report them. Numeral integrity is sound: every numeral used appears once in the table with a single meaning, every table entry appears on at least one figure, and no figure carries a numeral absent from the table. Section line 2-2 uses the same designation in FIG-1 (repeated at both ends with arrows), FIG-2's caption, and draft/07-drawings.md; all four broken-circle callouts (central, right-hand upper, right-hand lower, left-hand) are designated identically in FIG-2, in each enlarged view's brief, and in the Brief Description. No drafting note, placeholder, open question or unresolved alternative remains in draft/ or figures/, and no "by way of example" or "any closed outline" shape hedge leaked into the application text - the schematic conventions stay inside the figure briefs.
6	
7	Five findings, two critical. Both criticals are in figures/FIG-3.md, where the brief resolves an internal flow topology the inventor never disclosed. The disclosure says only that air "enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts". FIG-3 converts that into a specific route: each cassette "stops short of the upper web of the frame 42, leaving a blank open gap between its upper end and the underside of that web through which the space between the cassettes 44 communicates with the upper end of the duct 48 on that side", i.e. an over-the-top crossover from the inter-cassette space to the outboard ducts. FIG-3 also adds "a lower web portion of the frame 42 closing the underside of the frame 42 beneath each cassette 44 on each side of the opening 46", a flow boundary that forces that route. These are flow-path and contact-topology statements about a functional duct and port, so the "shown schematically" label does not excuse them; both must be removed and left unverbalized. Neither relationship appears anywhere in draft/08-detailed-description.md, so the figure would also depict structure the specification never describes.
8	
9	The major finding is in figures/FIG-6.md: the indicator housing is specified as "closed at its outer end" with a hatched (solid) body, which contradicts the disclosed and claimed behaviour that the indicator is "visible from outside" and that the spring moves the stem "to a latched exposed position" (claim 9, claim 17, description ¶45–47). The outer-end closure is itself untraced; deleting it resolves both the contradiction and the fidelity gap without adding any structure.
10	
11	Two minor findings: FIG-6 also states the spring's reaction surfaces and that it "is compressed", and places the latch "inside the housing" - an operating condition and relative locations the disclosure does not give (it says only that the stem is "retained by a temperature-responsive latch" and that "a spring moves the indicator stem"); and draft/10-abstract.md calls the shell an "insulated shell" where every other section, including claim 1, uses "insulated outer shell".
12	
13	No other internal inconsistency was verified. The description's flow order ("passes through the perforations ... and returns through the lower return passage") reproduces the inventor's own wording verbatim and the figure briefs deliberately leave the perforation locations unspecified, so I did not treat that as a drafting defect; resolving it would require adding undisclosed structure. Advantage and problem-framing prose in the description (e.g. "the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box") mirrors the Background and follows from the disclosed registration relationship, so it is not reported as an untraced result.
14

16	
17	- **Source fidelity is clean before rendering** (fail): Ledger scope: I traced every claim limitation (claims 1–17), every numeral in draft/numerals.md (10–86), and every structure, relationship, result, position, connection and operating condition in draft/04-field.md through draft/10-abstract.md and figures/FIG-1.md through FIG-6.md to the USER disclosure (input/disclosure.md, mirrored in the single USER passage of input/conversation.md). input/brief.md was used only for formalities (title is a "working title" so the descriptive title is acceptable; "No priority claim" and "No federally sponsored research" match the "Not applicable." cross-reference and government-support sections). prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the Background makes no citation, so nothing needed prior-art tracing.

Numeral integrity is sound: every numeral used ap
20	  - FIG-3 invents an over-the-top flow crossover from the inter-cassette space to the guide ducts
21	  - FIG-3 adds lower web portions closing the underside of the frame beneath each cassette
22	  - FIG-6 shows the indicator housing closed at its outer end, contradicting the disclosed exposed, externally visible indication
23	  - FIG-6 specifies untraced latch placement, spring reaction surfaces and a compressed spring state

27	
28	- **[critical] FIG-3 invents an over-the-top flow crossover from the inter-cassette space to the guide ducts** (figures/FIG-3.md, "Phase-change cassette 44" bullet (line 8)) - The brief specifies a particular internal flow route through the spacer frame: air reaches each downward guide duct 48 by passing over the top of the adjacent cassette 44 through a gap between the cassette's upper end and the underside of the frame's upper web. The disclosure describes only that air "enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts"; it never says how the space between the opposed cassettes communicates with the outboard ducts, never says a cassette stops short of any part of the frame, and never discloses an upper web closing the top of the inter-cassette space. This is a flow-path and flow-boundary relationship for a functional duct, so it is substantive notwithstanding the "schematic" framing, and it appears in no part of draft/08-detailed-description.md, meaning the figure would show a relationship the specification never describes.
29	  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-3.md, delete the sentence "Each cassette 44 stops short of the upper web of the frame 42, leaving a blank open gap between its upper end and the underside of that web through which the space between the cassettes 44 communicates with the upper end of the duct 48 on that side." and end the cassette bullet at "...each having an outboard surface facing the nearer outboard web." Retain the existing unnumbered bullet "The space between the two cassettes 44 is continuous with the opening 46 below it and communicates with both ducts 48, so that air entering the opening 46 passes along the opposed faces of the cassettes 44 and into the ducts 48.", which tracks the disclosed sequence without specifying an undisclosed crossover geometry.
30	- **[critical] FIG-3 adds lower web portions closing the underside of the frame beneath each cassette** (figures/FIG-3.md, "Rigid spacer frame 42" bullet (line 6) and "Central inlet opening 46" bullet (line 7)) - The brief specifies that the frame's underside is closed by lower web portions beneath each cassette on each side of the central inlet opening. That is a flow boundary: it prevents air from leaving the inter-cassette region downward except through the inlet, and together with the over-the-top gap it dictates the circulation route inside the module. The disclosure discloses only "a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes" with "a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings", and says nothing about the frame's web construction or which parts of its underside are closed. By contrast, the companion statement that the underside remains open at the lower end of each duct is traceable and should be kept.
31	  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-3.md, delete ", and short lower web portions," from the frame bullet so it reads "drawn as an upper horizontal web and an outboard upright web at each side of the view, continuous with one another"; and in the central inlet bullet delete "a lower web portion of the frame 42 closing the underside of the frame 42 beneath each cassette 44 on each side of the opening 46," so the bullet reads "...opening downward out of the underside of the frame 42 and upward into the blank open space between the two cassettes 44, the underside of the frame 42 remaining open at the lower end of each duct 48."
32	- **[major] FIG-6 shows the indicator housing closed at its outer end, contradicting the disclosed exposed, externally visible indication** (figures/FIG-6.md, "Mechanical exposure indicator 80" bullet (line 6), read against draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶45–) - The brief draws the indicator as a solid hatched box "closed at its outer end" with the stem's outer end lying inside it. If the outer end of the housing is closed and hatched, outward movement of the stem cannot produce an indication visible from outside, so the depiction contradicts the description and the claims, which require the indicator to be "visible from outside" and the spring to move the stem "to a latched exposed position". Section line 2-2 uses the same designation in FIG-1 (repeated at both ends with arrows), FIG-2's caption, and draft/07-drawings.md; all four broken-circle callouts (central, right-hand upper, right-hand lower, left-hand) are designated identically in FIG-2, in each enlarged view's brief, and in the Brief Description. content.content:
1	A reusable passive cold-chain carrier has an insulated shell, a removable product tray, a removable thermal module, and an insulated lid. Tray feet leave a return passage beneath the tray, whose side walls are spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages. The module is a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes and having a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts, and peripheral outlet openings. As the lid closes, a depending indexing rib enters a mating channel in the frame and shifts the module into a registered position in which the outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. Air circulates without a powered air mover, rising from the product region into the inlet opening, descending the guide ducts into the side supply passages, and returning through tray perforations and the return passage.

reasoning: Both critical items were flow-boundary statements inside the thermal module that the specification never describes. The disclosure says air enters the central inlet, divides along the cassette faces and descends the ducts, and stops there. FIG-3 had resolved that into a specific internal topology: an upper-end gap over each cassette plus a closed underside beneath each cassette, which together dictate the route. Deleting both leaves the disclosed sequence carried by the relationship line that says the inter-cassette space is continuous with the inlet and communicates with both ducts, which is the level of specificity the source actually supports.

I kept the companion statement that the underside of the frame remains open at the lower end of each duct, because that is traceable to the disclosed guide ducts opening at their lower ends and because FIG-4 places condensate discharge opening 56 there. Removing it would have created a new conflict between the two sheets while fixing nothing.

The FIG-6 housing finding was a functional contradiction, not just a fidelity gap. A hatched box closed at its outer end cannot show a stem that has moved to an exposed position visible from outside, which is what claim 9, claim 17 and the indicator paragraphs require. Deleting the closure clause fixes the contradiction and removes an undisclosed geometry in the same edit, without adding any replacement structure such as a window or an aperture that the inventor never described.

For the latch and spring I kept exactly the two things the source gives, that the latch retains the stem and that the spring acts outward on it, and dropped the rest: where the latch sits, what the spring bears against at each end, and whether it is compressed or extended. # FIG. 3

Enlarged schematic vertical section of the central upper region of the closed carrier indicated by the central broken circle in FIG. 2, on the same upright plane cutting from side to side, black line work on white, patent drawing style. Sectioned solids carry uniform diagonal hatching; open spaces are blank. Keep all line work well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

- Insulated lid 60: a horizontal hatched slab of substantial thickness spanning the top of the view.
- Rigid spacer frame 42: a hatched frame body of visible wall thickness below the lid 60, drawn as an upper horizontal web and an outboard upright web at each side of the view, continuous with one another.
- Central inlet opening 46: the blank open region at the centre of the width of the frame 42, open downward at the underside of the frame 42 toward the tray and continuous upward with the blank open space between the two cassettes 44.
- Phase-change cassette 44: two upright slab-like bodies held within the frame 42, one on each side of the opening 46, each with its own outline and hatching pattern distinct from that of the frame 42, facing one another across a blank open space directly above the opening 46, each having an outboard surface facing the nearer outboard web.
- Downward guide duct 48: two blank open upright passages, one on each side, each between the outboard surface of one cassette 44 and the nearer outboard web of the frame 42, each open at its lower end at the bottom of the view.
- Mating channel 52: an upwardly open recess in the upper web of the frame 42, shown schematically and bounded on both sides by hatched frame material.

- The rib 62 is engaged in the channel 52 while the lid 60 lies above the upper web of the frame 42.

All three findings are fixed.

- **FIG-3 central inlet opening 46 (major):** the bullet no longer describes a rectangular gap cut in a frame underside the brief does not draw. It now reads as the blank open region at the centre of the width of the frame, open downward at the underside toward the tray and continuous upward with the space between the two cassettes. The duplicate clause about the underside at the duct lower ends is gone, since the duct bullet already states that each duct is open at its lower end, and the flow relationship line is unchanged.
- **FIG-6 stem 82 (minor):** the closing relationship line no longer places the stem's inner end at the cassette. It now has the stem running from the interior of the housing of the indicator 80 through the shell side wall 14, its inner end lying at the inner side of that wall and thermally coupled to the cassette 44 shown at the right of the view, with the intervening structure omitted. That matches the stem bullet and matches the "thermally coupled" wording of the description and claim 9, without asserting contact.
- **FIG-5 pull tab 74 (minor):** both the tab bullet and the closing relationship line now condition accessibility on the removable product tray being removed, and both use the full designation.

No application text, numeral or drawing description needed changing: the description keeps the inlet shape-neutral and already conditions the tab on tray removal, so nothing was out of step. Every brief is under 2800 characters, each numeral list still matches what its brief verbalizes, and the numeral table is unchanged.

input.summary: Fixed all three figure-brief findings: FIG-3's central inlet opening 46 is now the blank open region at the centre of the frame width rather than a rectangular gap cut in an undrawn frame underside, FIG-6's closing relationship line now places the stem's inner end at the inner side of the shell side wall and states thermal coupling rather than contact with the cassette, and FIG-5 now conditions the pull tab's accessibility on removal of the removable product tray in both places it is mentioned.
reasoning: The FIG-3 item was a drawability trap that would have forced back the exact flow boundary removed last round. Specifying a gap opening downward out of the frame's underside, when the frame bullet draws only an upper web and two outboard webs, leaves a renderer no option but to invent lower web material on each side of the inlet. Describing the inlet as the blank open region at the centre of the frame width removes that pressure while keeping everything the source gives: an inlet at the centre of the frame, open downward toward the tray, continuous with the space between the cassettes.

I also dropped the inlet bullet's clause about the underside remaining open at the lower end of each duct. The duct bullet already states that each duct is open at its lower end, so the clause added nothing and was a second place where the brief talked about which parts of the frame underside are open, which is not something the inventor characterizes.

"Rectangular" went with it. The description keeps the inlet shape-neutral as an opening at the centre of the frame facing the product region, so an outline for a functional port had no source and no counterpart in the text the figure illustrates.

FIG-6 had the stem ending in two different places in two bullets, and the second one converted thermal coupling into physical contact. The disclosure, description paragraph 45 and claim 9 all say only that the stem is thermally coupled to one cassette, so the relationship line now states the coupling without asserting that the stem touches the cassette, and puts the inner end where the stem bullet already put it. Referring to the interior of the housing of the indicator 80 also keeps numeral 80 meaning the whole indicator, as the numeral table and claim 9 have it.

FIG-5's closing line asserted flatly that the tab is reachable from above in a view that draws the closed carrier with the tray in place. The disclosure conditions accessibility on the tray being removed, and the tab bullet already said so, so the condition now appears in both statements with the full part designation.

Nothing in the claims, description, drawing descriptions or numeral table had to move. The description never recited an inlet shape, never described the frame's web construction, and already conditions the tab on tray removal, so the briefs were the only files out of step with the text they illustrate.
changes: figures/FIG-3.md: central inlet opening 46 bullet replaced with 'the blank open region at the centre of the width of the frame 42, open downward at the underside of the frame 42 toward the tray and continuous upward with the blank open space between the two cassettes 44', removing the rectangular outline, the gap-in-the-underside construction, and the duplicate clause about the underside at the lower end of each duct.

figures/FIG-6.md: closing relationship line replaced with 'The stem 82 extends from the interior of the housing of the indicator 80 through the thickness of the shell side wall 14, its inner end lying at the inner side of the shell side wall 14 and being thermally coupled to the cassette 44 shown at the right of the view, the intervening structure being omitted.'

figures/FIG-5.md: pull tab 74 bullet now reads 'when the removable product tray is removed'; closing relationship line replaced with 'The wick 72 lies in the trough of the channel 70 along its length, and the tab 74 is drawn so as to be accessible from above when the removable product tray is removed.'
input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the Background carries no citations, so no prior-art tracing or design-around was required this round. The combination the specification develops is untouched: the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel as the lid closes shifts the removable thermal module into the registered position where the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, establishing a closed, fan-free circulation path around the removable product tray and between two opposed phase-change cassettes, with the specification explaining the problem that solves, a displaced module that silently reduces the carrier to a plain insulated box. Claim 1 recites the central inlet opening, the ducts, the outlet openings and their overlap rather than any frame web construction or port outline, so removing those details from FIG-3 does not touch claim scope. Because no prior-art search was run, the art available to this draft may be incomplete.

FIG-6 no longer contradicts itself about where the indicator stem ends and no longer asserts stem-to-cassette contact: the stem runs from the interior of the housing of the indicator through the shell side wall, its inner end at the inner side of that wall and thermally coupled to the cassette, with the intervening structure omitted. FIG-5 conditions the pull tab's accessibility on removal of the removable product tray in both the tab bullet and the closing relationship line. No claim, description passage, drawing description, numeral definition or disclosed embodiment changed, each brief's numeral list still matches what it verbalizes, no sheet lists more than eight numerals, and every brief is under 2800 characters.
